distinguishing_features: Modifies die taper geometry to redistribute contact pressure, rather than using a sensor/telemetry inference scheme
Treats abrasion erosion as a physical contact-pressure problem at the die-wire interface, not a monitoring-only indication
Delivers a hardware design change (reground taper angle) as the active ingredient, whereas all prior art delivers software-based normalization/inference of existing signals
Fundamental physics differs: contact-pressure redistribution in a conical drawing die versus motor-current or pressure-drop fault inference
parsed.objective_technical_problem: How to physically reduce localized abrasion erosion on the die-wire contact surface (lower peak contact pressure below the scratch threshold) rather than merely detecting scratches after they occur.
parsed.viable_reason: The stated governing relation p ∝ 1/(r² sin α) is dimensionally and physically garbled, and the candidate conflates reducing cone angle with spreading load, whereas a shallower taper angle in a drawing die actually tends to increase contact length/normal pressure at fixed reduction; the claimed 35% pressure drop and 500 MPa scratch threshold are unverified and the mechanism is not convincingly demonstrated as feasible at the stated scale.
parsed.non_obvious_reason: Even if the geometry change were sound, reducing a die taper angle is a routine parameter/geometry adjustment a skilled die designer would make; the distinguishing step is not a non-obvious departure from ordinary tribological practice.
